Predicates:
GoodGuys(x) ::: x are the good guys.
Win(x, y) ::: x wins y.
Fight(x, y) ::: x fights y.
Nemesis(x, y) ::: x is nemesis of y.
NamedAfter(x, y) ::: x is named after y.
InMovie(x, y) ::: x is in the movie y.
Character(x) ::: x is a character.
Movie(x) ::: x is a movie.
Name(x, y) ::: x is named y.
Fights(x, y) ::: x fights y.
Winners(x, y) ::: x wins y.
TheMovie(y) ::: y is a superhero movie.
GoodGuysWin(y) ::: in movie y, the good guys always win.

Premises:
∀x (GoodGuys(x) → Win(x, y)) ::: In superhero movies, the good guys always win.
TheMovie(surprisingAdventures) ::: The Surprising Adventures of Sir Digby Chicken Caesar is a superhero movie.
Fight(sirDigby, nemesis) ::: Sir Digby fights his nemesis.
NamedAfter(surprisingAdventures, sirDigby) ::: The Surprising Adventures of Sir Digby Chicken Caesar is named after Sir Digby.
Name(surprisingAdventures, sirDigby) ::: The movie is named after Sir Digby.
InMovie(sirDigby, surprisingAdventures) ::: Sir Digby is in the movie.
Fight(sirDigby, nemesis) ::: Sir Digby fights his nemesis.
∃x (Character(x) ∧ Name(x, sirDigby) ∧ InMovie(x, y)) ::: if a character is named after Sir Digby, then that character is in the movie.
∀x (Fight(x, y) → ¬Win(x, y)) ::: If somebody fights someone, then the fighter does not win the fight.

Conclusion:
¬Win(nemesis, sirDigby) ::: Sir Digby's nemesis does not win.
